title: Skills Children Need for an AI-Powered Future
metaDescription: Five adaptable skills worth building now: critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, digital literacy and self-regulation, with practical activities.

sections.heading: Build capabilities, not job predictions
paragraphs: Nobody can say with confidence which specific jobs will exist when today's children are adults, and plenty of adults have learned not to trust the predictions that circulated even five or ten years ago. What's more useful than a guess about future jobs is a short list of capabilities that hold up well whatever that future turns out to look like: thinking critically about information, working well with other people, being creative inside real constraints, using digital tools (including AI tools) sensibly, and managing your own learning. None of these are new - good teachers and parents have cultivated them for decades - but they matter more, not less, in a world where generating plausible-sounding text and images is suddenly cheap and instant.

This article is about building those five capabilities directly, mostly away from any screen. It's a companion to - not a substitute for - Money Quest's articles that focus specifically on AI and money together; here, money shows up only occasionally, as one example among several, because the skills themselves are broader than any single domain.

sections.heading: Critical thinking and verification
paragraphs: A practical way in is to make checking a claim feel normal rather than confrontational. Give a child two different answers to the same question - one right, one subtly wrong - and ask which one they'd trust and why, rather than simply telling them which is correct. The useful skill isn't spotting this particular error; it's getting comfortable with the question 'what would convince me either way?'

It's just as important to make revising a view feel normal, not like losing an argument. When new information changes the picture, say so out loud yourself - 'I thought X, but this new information changes my mind, so now I think Y' - so children see an adult model changing course without treating it as a defeat.

sections.heading: Communication and collaboration
paragraphs: A useful task asks a small group to design a low-cost community service - a shared tool library, a lift-sharing rota, a repair café. Each child contributes an idea, listens to someone else's, and has to explain a decision the group makes, which is a genuinely different skill from just having a good idea alone.

Making this genuinely inclusive takes a bit more than good intentions. Allow spoken, typed, drawn, and AAC (augmentative and alternative communication) contributions side by side within the same task, so a child who communicates through a device or through drawing is contributing on equal footing with a child who's comfortable speaking up. For a child who needs longer to process a question or formulate a response, build in a real pause before moving on - some children will also do better contributing in writing first and sharing it rather than being asked to think aloud in the moment. None of these adjustments change what's being assessed; they change who gets a fair chance to show it.

sections.heading: Creativity with constraints
paragraphs: Ask children to solve a real problem using only three available materials, or a fictional £20 budget (this is a UK-style example in pounds; adapt the currency and amount for your own context). The constraint is doing the work here, not the budget itself - it's just one convenient way to force comparison between options. A tight limit makes children compare trade-offs and explain their reasoning, rather than producing an endless list of ideas with no way to choose between them.

The same approach works with time limits, material limits, or a 'must include everyone's idea in some form' rule instead of a budget - the underlying skill is choosing well under a real constraint, and money is simply one familiar constraint among several that work equally well.

sections.heading: Digital and AI literacy
paragraphs: Children benefit from an early, concrete understanding that AI systems can generate plausible-sounding text and images while still making mistakes, reflecting biases in the material they were built from, or mishandling personal information. The most effective way to teach this with younger children is through adult-led demonstrations using fictional prompts, rather than open independent use - UNESCO's guidance for generative AI in education specifically recommends age-appropriate, adult-supervised approaches and age limits for independent use of general-purpose AI tools (https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/guidance-generative-ai-education-and-research).

In practice, that means children should not be set up with independent accounts on general-purpose AI services, and any AI output they see should be framed from the start as something to check, not something to trust by default.

sections.heading: Self-regulation and reflection
paragraphs: A simple cycle - plan, try, check, improve - gives children a repeatable structure for almost any task, including ones that have nothing to do with money or technology. After an activity, ask what worked and what they'd change next time, and treat the answer as useful information rather than a formality to get through before moving on.

This kind of explicit modelling and guided reflection has a stronger evidence base than simply assuming these habits develop on their own from screen time or general life experience - the Education Endowment Foundation's review of metacognition and self-regulation strategies finds that teaching pupils to plan, monitor and evaluate their own learning has a consistently positive, moderate effect, when it's taught explicitly rather than left implicit (https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/metacognition-and-self-regulation).

sections.heading: Worked example: a decision children can explain
paragraphs: A class wants to reduce paper waste. Teams propose a system for reusing scrap paper, estimate roughly what it would cost to set up, and test the idea for one week. Children plan the system, monitor what actually happens once it's running, and explain afterwards what they'd change. AI tools are optional here and shouldn't replace the children's own reasoning - if a team uses one to brainstorm options, the group still has to evaluate and choose between them itself.

sections.heading: Facilitator's step-by-step plan
list: Define a real, small problem in child-friendly terms, with no single 'correct' answer already in mind.
Ask each team for two solutions with genuinely different costs or constraints, not just two versions of the same idea.
Test one idea safely over a short, fixed period and record what actually happened, not just what was predicted.
Review the evidence together and change the plan if it doesn't hold up - treat this as the point of the exercise, not a sign it went wrong.

sections.heading: How to check understanding
paragraphs: The clearest sign a child has actually built these skills, rather than just enjoyed the activity, is being able to describe a decision they changed after seeing new evidence - not simply having their first idea praised and left unchallenged. Ask directly: 'what did you think at the start, and what's different now?' A child who can answer that is demonstrating revision, which is the actual skill being taught.

It's also worth checking whether a child can apply the same reasoning habit to an unfamiliar problem, not just the one just practised - a child who only ever compares options in the exact format they were taught hasn't yet generalised the underlying skill.

sections.heading: Common teaching mistakes to avoid
list: Avoid presenting predictions about specific future jobs as settled fact - nobody genuinely knows, and treating a guess as certain undermines the more useful message about adaptable habits.
Avoid letting 'AI literacy' mean only tool fluency - knowing how to prompt a system well is far less important than knowing when to question its output.
Avoid rewarding only the first idea a child produces; reward the process of comparing, checking and revising, since that's the transferable part.

Avoid treating this as a separate AI-safety topic - online safety and AI-specific risks are covered in Money Quest's dedicated AI-safety articles; this article's angle is building the underlying thinking and collaboration skills that make a child better equipped generally, with or without AI in the picture.

sections.heading: Try this next
paragraphs: Pick one activity from this guide and run it with a different fictional scenario - a different constraint, a different small problem to solve. Ask the child to explain a decision they changed their mind about, in whichever way suits them best - spoken, written, drawn or through an AAC device - and keep any real family or school details private by using fictional names and figures.

sections.heading: Editorial references
paragraphs: Guidance on age-appropriate, adult-supervised approaches to generative AI in education draws on UNESCO's Guidance for generative AI in education and research: https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/guidance-generative-ai-education-and-research. The evidence on teaching planning, monitoring and evaluation explicitly draws on the Education Endowment Foundation's Metacognition and self-regulation guidance: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/metacognition-and-self-regulation.

faqs.question: How long should one of these activities take?
faqs.answer: Start with a short session of around ten to fifteen minutes, then adapt to the group's attention span and the complexity of the problem chosen. This is a practical starting point rather than a research-established optimum.

faqs.question: What if a child gives an answer I didn't expect?
faqs.answer: Ask for the reasoning behind it, check that the task itself was understood as intended, and offer another example if needed. An unexpected answer that's well-reasoned is often more useful to discuss than a predictable 'correct' one.

faqs.question: Should children be using AI tools directly for these activities?
faqs.answer: For most of these activities, no independent account or direct access is needed, and younger children in particular benefit more from adult-led demonstrations with fictional prompts than from open-ended independent use. Where an older child does use an AI tool as part of a task, treat its output as a starting point to question, not a finished answer.

faqs.question: Why does money only come up occasionally in this article?
faqs.answer: The five skills here - critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, digital literacy and self-regulation - are broader than any one domain, so money appears only as one convenient, familiar constraint for the creativity activity. Money Quest covers AI and money together in more depth in its other articles on that specific topic.
